newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices jump on concerns about supplies.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices jump on concerns about supplies.

text.p: Coffee prices jumped to the highest level in seven months Tuesday after warehouse stocks of coffee unexpectedly fell and news from South America pointed to smaller crops.
Grain prices rose for a second day on weather concerns, and oil prices took a break from their prolonged rally.
At the New York Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, March coffee closed 5.30 cents a pound higher at 119.35 cents, its highest closing price since May 20.

The market rose from the start after the exchange in its weekly update Monday reported that coffee stocks in U.S. warehouses certified for delivery against CSCE futures fell by 1,607 132-pound bags in the week ended Friday to 32,458 bags.
Selling of futures by producing countries seeking to price their coffee kept a cap on the surge, but heavy buying by commodity fund investors later drove prices higher.

That buying was sparked when a Brazilian official told Reuters in Rio de Janeiro that Brazil's government was working with a range of between 18.5 million and 19.5 million bags for the 1997/98 coffee crop -- much smaller than the prior year's crop, dealers said. The official stressed those numbers were not an official estimate.
"There was pretty good fund buying," said Steve Platt, a Dean Witter analyst in Chicago. "The late move was helped by the Brazil numbers. With the reductions, stocks are going to remain tight.
Brazil had a 26.5 million-bag crop last year, Platt said.
Adding to bullish sentiment was news that Costa Rica's 1996/97 coffee production may fall 6.2 percent to 2.3 million bags from 2.6 million bags in 1995/96.
The Costa Rica Coffee Institute said the expected decrease in production was due to a cyclical decline and damage from Hurricane Cesar that ravaged crop areas last fall.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, weather concerns pushed grain prices higher.
March wheat closed 4 cents a bushel higher at $3.92-1/2 on fears that the return of bitter cold to the Midwest and Plains might damage the dormant winter wheat crop.

January soybeans closed 4-1/2 cents a bushel higher at $6.98-1/2 on the belief that hot, dry weather in Brazil may hurt the young crop there. March corn closed 1-1/4 cents a bushel higher at $2.58-1/4 on concerns about hot weather in Argentina, but some months closed lower on reports of rains in the wheat-exporting country.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, a prolonged rally that has taken oil prices near post-Gulf War highs paused amid expectations of a rise in U.S. heating oil stocks to rise in weekly data due out after the close.
February heating oil closed down 1.15 cents a gallon at 72.49 cents.

The American Petroleum Institute reported after the market closed that stocks of distillates, which include heating oil and diesel fuel, rose 2.94 million barrels in the week ended Friday. Traders had expected distillate stocks to rise by more than a million barrels.
Crude and gasoline were caught in heating oil's downdraft with February crude closing down 14 cents at $26.23 a barrel, and February gasoline down 0.42 cent at 72.10 cents a gallon.
